function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse and the constraints of your experiment.** Below is a quick guide to help you decide which technique might suit your needs best. | Ionisation Method | Typical Applications | Advantages | Disadvantages | Ideal Use‑Case | |-------------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|----------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Simple, robust;
• Produces reproducible fragmentation patterns;
• Good for library matching. | • Requires high vacuum;
• Not suitable for large or labile molecules;
• Generates only singly charged ions. | Routine GC‑MS analysis of small organic compounds. | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Semi‑volatile organics, pharmaceuticals, natural products. | • Soft ionisation → less fragmentation;
• Can produce protonated or deprotonated molecules;
• Compatible with GC‑MS. | • Requires a reagent gas;
• Lower sensitivity for some analytes. | Quantitative GC‑MS where minimal fragmentation is desired. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Lipids, steroids, small peptides, polar organics. | • Operates at atmospheric pressure;
• Handles moderately polar compounds;
• Good for LC‑MS. | • Less effective for very polar or large biomolecules;
• Requires a solvent that can be vaporised. | LC‑MS of lipids, steroids, and other semi‑polar analytes. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Proteins, peptides, nucleic acids, large biomolecules. | • Very soft ionisation;
• Produces multiply charged ions → extends mass range;
• Compatible with LC‑MS. | • Requires aqueous solvents;
• Susceptible to ion suppression from salts. | LC‑MS/MS of proteins, peptides, metabolites, and complex mixtures. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteins, polymers, large biomolecules, imaging. | • Handles very large molecules;
• Minimal fragmentation;
• Fast analysis;
• Imaging capability. | • Requires matrix preparation;
• Limited to solid samples;
• Lower resolution for small molecules. | MALDI‑TOF MS of proteins, peptides, polymers, and tissue imaging. | | **Laser Desorption Ionisation (LDI)** | Polymers, inorganic materials. | • No matrix needed;
• Useful for non‑polar, high‑molecular‑weight species. | • Often produces singly charged ions;
• Less common. | Analysis of polymers or inorganic solids. | | **Field‑Ionisation (FII)** | Small molecules, high‑resolution MS. | • Ultra‑soft ionisation;
• Produces singly charged ions with minimal fragmentation. | • Requires specialized equipment;
• Limited throughput. | High‑resolution MS of small, thermally labile molecules. | ### How to Pick 1. **Sample Size & Complexity** - *Small, volatile*: EI or CI (GC‑MS). - *Large, polar, or biomolecules*: ESI or MALDI (LC‑MS). 2. **Desired Fragmentation** - *Library matching*: EI (good fragmentation). - *Minimal fragmentation*: CI, APCI, or MALDI. 3. **Instrument Availability** - Many labs have LC‑MS with ESI/APCI; GC‑MS with EI/CI. - MALDI‑TOF is common in proteomics labs. 4. **Quantitation vs. Identification** - For quantitative work, softer ionisation (CI, APCI, ESI) often yields better reproducibility. - For structural elucidation, EI or ESI with tandem MS (MS/MS) is preferred. 5. **Special Requirements** - *Imaging*: MALDI imaging. - *Very high‑resolution*: FII or high‑resolution ESI. --- #### Quick Decision Flow ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the sample small & volatile? ──► Yes → EI (GC‑MS) │ │ │ ▼ │ No → Is it a large biomolecule? ──► Yes → ESI (LC‑MS/MS) or MALDI‑TOF │ │ │ ▼ │ No → Is it a semi‑polar organic? ──► Yes → APCI (LC‑MS) or CI (GC‑MS) │ │ │ ▼ │ No → Consider MALDI imaging or specialized methods ``` --- ### Bottom Line - **For routine GC‑MS of small organics:** **EI** (most common). - **For LC‑MS of proteins/peptides:** **ESI** (soft, multiplies charge). - **For lipidomics or semi‑polar compounds:** **APCI** (soft, good for LC‑MS). - **For imaging or very large biomolecules:** **MALDI** (solid‑phase, imaging). If you give me more details about your sample type, matrix, and analytical goals, I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
